Acknowledgements: We thank the Kleine Weltentdecker*innen Lab and the Jacobs Center for Productive Youth Development at Universität Zürich for providing the resources necessary for this research and all children and their caregivers for their participation in our studies. Next to that, we want to thank Chiara Carrel, Merve Bot, and Deborah Lamm for their effort and contribution to the project. This work was partially funded by the Jacobs Foundation.

The Associations between Social Network Size and Preschool Children's Visual Perspective-Taking and Non-Verbal Cue Understanding

Communicative behaviour enables us to navigate our daily interactions and relationships (Gampe et al., 2019; Schmerse et al., 2015). Communication is particularly important for children, as it connects them with their environment and fosters their language, cognitive, and emotional development (Saarni et al., 2007; Vaccari & Marschark, 1997). At the same time, children's communicative behaviour does not develop independently of this environment. The people children interact with, and the diversity of these social experiences, may shape how they communicate (Wermelinger et al., 2024). Therefore, children's social networks represent an aspect of their everyday communicative environment. However, how diversity in children's social networks is associated to their communicative behaviour remains relatively underexplored. Effective communication requires a broad set of behaviours, including language knowledge (Brodin & Renblad, 2020), turn-taking conventions (Cosper & Pika, 2025), (visual) perspective-taking (Keysar et al., 2000), and understanding of non-verbal cues such as gestures (Tomasello, 2003). Together, these skills form children's pragmatic communication behaviour: the ability to use and interpret language appropriately within its social context (Bohn & Frank, 2019). Acquiring these behaviours is demanding, and children vary in how and when they develop them (Wermelinger et al., 2024). Understanding what drives this variation is important, both theoretically and practically, as early communicative behaviour predicts later social and academic outcomes (Denham et al., 2003; Mcclelland et al., 2007). In the next paragraphs, we explain how three important abilities in communication (i.e., theory of mind, visual perspective-taking, and non-verbal cue understanding) develop, and are related to children's social environments.

Theory of Mind and Visual Perspective-Taking

A central component of communicative behaviour is Theory of Mind (ToM), which is the understanding and reasoning about other people's mental states and how these states influence their behaviour (Rakoczy, 2022). ToM is not a unitary construct but encompasses a range of precursors, from perceptual perspective-taking to reasoning about beliefs, intentions, and emotions (Wellman, 2014). These precursors emerge and develop at different rates over early childhood and may be shaped by distinct experiential drivers (Meinhardt-Injac et al., 2020; Westby & Robinson, 2014). This heterogeneity is also reflected in how they are typically measured: separate abilities such as visual perspective-taking or false-belief understanding are usually assessed with lab-based tasks, whereas caregiver questionnaires are used to assess all or multiple precursors of ToM in a single measure. The two show only modest convergent validity in early childhood (Dore et al., 2015). This distinction matters for interpreting how social experience may differentially shape different ToM precursors.

One salient ToM component is visual perspective-taking, which is essential for effective communication (Keysar et al., 2000). Around nine months, children engage in joint attention, understanding that others may see things they themselves do not see; this reflects Level I perspective-taking. Then, by around 4 years, children typically understand that others can perceive the same object but interpret it differently from their own perspective (Level II perspective-taking ; Flavell, 2004).

The director task is a widely used measure of visual perspective-taking (Agostini et al., 2024a; Fan et al., 2015; Keysar et al., 2000; Lin et al., 2010). In this task, a child and an experimenter (i.e., the director) share a grid of objects. Because of their opposite seating positions, some objects are occluded from the director's view, but visible to the child. The child receives an instruction from the director that is ambiguous from the child's own perspective but unambiguous from the director's (see Figure1. Correctly answering the director's request requires the child to inhibit their own perspective and infer what the director can see. This places simultaneous demands on perspective-taking and inhibitory control, making it a sensitive measure of communicative role-taking (Fan et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2010). Performance on the director task is associated with the environment in which children grow up. In this task, bilingual 4-year-olds outperformed their monolingual peers (Agostini et al., 2024b; Fan et al., 2015). This suggests that diverse linguistic experience enhances the ability to ignore or suppress one's own perspective (Liberman et al., 2017) and favour the other's perspective. However, the mechanism driving this advantage is debated: some accounts emphasise inhibitory control (Agostini et al., 2024b), while others point to the broader communicative diversity that bilingual environments provide (Wermelinger et al., 2024).

Greater social diversity, as indexed by children's weekly social network size, is associated with higher performance on the director task (Burke et al., 2023). This is consistent with the perspective that experiencing greater communicative diversity supports perspective-taking (Wermelinger et al., 2024).

For similar findings on the associations between children's environment and their ToM, see Farhadian et al. (2010), Hughes and Leekam (2004), Lewis et al. (1996) and Schroeder (2018). The results from these studies follow a pattern similar to perspective-taking and non-verbal cue understanding: greater diversity in children's environments is associated with improved performance on ToM tasks. This suggests that the number and variety of people children interact with may play a role in their ToM development, which is important for the effectiveness of their communication (Meltzoff, 1999; Sidera et al., 2018).

Non-Verbal Cue Understanding

Besides being able to take another person's perspective, successful communication requires the integration of different sources of information (Tomasello, 2003), such as the literal meaning of speech, non-verbal cues, and the situational context (Baldwin, 1995; Hollich et al., 2000). Especially when verbal information is ambiguous or absent, interlocutors rely on cues such as gaze direction and pointing to establish shared reference (Bohn et al., 2019; Tomasello, 2003). Understanding these cues requires children to monitor multiple sources of information simultaneously and to interpret cues flexibly depending on the context (Baldwin, 1995). Bilinguals demonstrate heightened sensitivity to ambiguous referential cues (Yow & Markman, 2011), particularly in the most challenging condition: situations involving subtle, ambiguous non-verbal cues. In a task in which children were asked to find a hidden marble in one of two opaque boxes, bilinguals outperformed monolinguals on trials where the experimenter's body position was opposite her gaze direction (Yow & Markman, 2011). Further, bilingual children rely more strongly on non-verbal information than their monolingual peers (Lauro et al., 2020). Bilinguals need to constantly monitor their partner's language use, which increases the risk of communicative breakdown. It is suggested that, to compensate for this, children may direct more attention to non-verbal cues to prevent communicative breakdowns (Yow & Markman, 2011). The bilingual advantage in non-verbal cue understanding may, therefore, arise not from language knowledge itself but from the demands of navigating communicatively diverse environments.

Taken together, the differences observed between monolingual and bilingual children's communicative behaviour in visual perspective-taking tasks, ToM, and non-verbal cue understanding do not have to arise from language per se but could be driven by the greater diversity these communicative environments provide (Paradis, 2023). The COMmunicative Experience (COME) perspective (Wermelinger et al., 2024) proposes that exposure to a wide variety of communicative situations (e.g., the number of different partners, their personal characteristics and familiarity to the child, the frequency and length of interactions, languages used in these interactions) drives the development of a broader, more flexible communicative repertoire. Children who encounter challenging communicative situations more frequently (e.g., because of limited language proficiency or cultural differences in how meaning is expressed) develop more varied strategies for making communication effective. Bilingual environments, with their demands for constant monitoring of a partner's language and proficiency, increase the likelihood of communicative breakdown and provide more opportunities for repair, thereby promoting communicative flexibility (Wermelinger et al., 2024). Critically, the COME perspective predicts that any source of communicative diversity not only bilingualism, could produce developmental advantages, as it generates more variation in communicative demands. This includes aspects of children's social networks such as the number of interaction partners and their personal characteristics, the interaction frequency, and length (see sections Non-Verbal Cue Understanding and Theory of Mind and Visual Perspective-Taking).

However, until now, bilingualism has received substantially more research attention than these other sources of communicative diversity.

Social Network Size as a Source of Diversity

Children's social networks, defined by the number and variety of people and groups they interact with, are one source of diversity in communicative environments.

Despite an increase in the number of studies on children's and adolescent social networks (e.g., Cooc & Kim, 2017; Neal & Veenstra, 2021), social networks have received comparatively little attention in early childhood, and the first methods for measuring social network size (SNS) in this age group have only recently been introduced (Burke et al., 2022). How SNS is best operationalised, particularly regarding which contacts should be included, therefore remains unsettled. Nonetheless, a larger and more varied social network may shape communicative development through the demands it places on children's interactions (Wermelinger et al., 2024). Through repeated interaction, partners build common ground: the accumulation of shared knowledge, experiences, and communicative conventions that make interaction more efficient over time (Bohn & Köymen, 2018; Clark & Brennan, 1991). When common ground is limited, as it is with less familiar partners, interlocutors cannot rely on it and must attend more carefully to a wider range of communicative cues to achieve mutual understanding instead (Bohn & Köymen, 2018; Branigan et al., 2016). Children with smaller social networks encounter these situations less, since they simply do not meet less familiar people often. In contrast, children with larger and more varied social networks are more likely to interact with partners with whom they share little common ground, placing greater and more varied demands on their communicative behaviour (Wermelinger et al., 2024).

Consistent with this, social network size is positively associated with visual perspective-taking in both children (Burke et al., 2023) and adults (Stiller & Dunbar, 2007). Burke et al. (2023) found that 3-year-olds with larger social networks performed better on a Level I perspective-taking task, particularly in trials requiring inference about the experimenter's hidden view. Further, children in kindergarten with mixed-age groups performed better on false-belief ToM tasks than those in same-age groups (Wang & Su, 2009), which supports the hypothesis that social diversity shapes children's communicative development. Whether this extends to non-verbal cue understanding remains untested. Given that visual perspective-taking and non-verbal cue understanding are thought to develop through communicative experience (Ruffman et al., 2002; Wermelinger et al., 2024), and that bilingual advantages have been documented in both domains, social network size is a theoretically motivated predictor.

The Present Study

The present study is a cross-sectional behavioural investigation with three primary goals. First, we aim to replicate the findings of Burke et al. (2023) by examining the relationship between children's social network size and their visual perspective-taking. Second, we seek to extend these findings by including an older sample and by employing a more demanding perspective-taking task involving ambiguous instructions, thereby targeting Level II perspective-taking. Third, we aim to test the hypothesis that children's social network size is associated with their understanding of non-verbal cues. Evidence for this relationship would support the assumption that social diversity, similar to diversity arising from bilingualism, facilitates the development of pragmatic communication behaviours. In addition, we apply an exploratory data-driven approach to determine the minimum annual interaction frequency needed for a relationship to meaningfully contribute to a child's social network size. We then examine how this network size predicts perspective-taking and non-verbal cue understanding. Further, we will explore the association between social network size and the wider construct of Theory of Mind. We analyse data from parental questionnaires, a visual perspective-taking task and a non-verbal cue understanding task from a study conducted in our research group between March and November 2025.

Methods

We preregistered the study prior to data analysis (https://osf.io/hgr98/?view_only=8c2484c223754b89b7d8ed80e35317d8) and made the collected data and R codes available on the Open Science Framework (see Data Availability Statement). All deviations from the preregistration are explicitly noted.

Participants

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study. The current study is part of a larger project, preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) under https://osf.io/dm94h/overview?view_only=91d93f4e097a4a71aa7ca80ba0fea81e. Therefore, we did not conduct an a priori power analysis for this study. The final sample consisted of N = 128 children, aged 3.5 to 4.5 years (M age = 4.06 years, SD age = 0.29), of whom 48.4% were female. We conducted a post hoc sensitivity analysis to determine the smallest detectable effect size with 80% power given our final sample. This indicated we could detect effects of OR ≥ 1.52 for social network size as a predictor of performance for the director task and OR ≥ 1.36 for the point-or-gaze task, and Cohen's f 2 of 0.06 on the questionnaire assessing children's ToM. We interpret null results with these thresholds in mind (see Results).

Children's language background (monolingual, bilingual, or bidialectal, categorised following Wermelinger et al. (2017) based on caregiver-reported language exposure; see Language Exposure) was not associated with social network size (F (2, 121) = 1.00, p = .371, R² = .02). Language status was also unrelated to performance on the director task, the point-or-gaze task, or the CSUS (see S2 in the supplementary materials). This supports our focus on SNS as a source of communicative diversity, independent of language status. The participating children largely came from families with relatively high socio-economic backgrounds: 81.5% of caregivers indicated above average, or average earnings (8.9%), and 5.6% earned below the city's mean income level for households with children (Bundesamt fuer Statistik, 2024), 4.0% did not answer. Parental educational attainment was similarly high. In 79.8% of families, both caregivers had completed higher education at either a university or a university of applied sciences. In 15.3% of families, one caregiver held such a degree. 4.8% of caregivers reported both caregivers having vocational training or apprenticeships as their educational background. Participants were recruited from the research unit's database, which includes caregivers who had previously expressed interest in participating in research with their children. Children born healthy, at term (>37 weeks of gestation), with a birth weight above 2500 grams, and no reported developmental disorders were invited to participate in the study. Each child received a certificate of participation and a gift (approximately USD 5,-) for their participation. Caregivers provided informed consent for participation. The Ethics Committee of the University of Zurich approved the general procedure, which followed the ethical standards of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments. Each session was videotaped and coded from the recording.

Procedure

The study took place in the lab of the Department of Psychology at the University of Zurich. The language of testing was the societal language, Swiss German.

Children visited the lab, accompanied by one caregiver and were welcomed by the experimenter. In the lab's playroom, the experimenter explained the study procedure to the caregiver, who provided written consent. The lab visit lasted approximately 45 minutes. After a familiarisation period in the playroom, the experimenter guided the child and their caregiver to the study room, where the caregiver was given a tablet and asked to complete online questionnaires on demographic information, the child's language exposure and the child's Theory of Mind (see Methods, as well as their own cultural values (House et al., 2004, the GLOBE (irrelevant to the current study), ).

Meanwhile, the child participated in the director task and the non-verbal cue understanding task. Further, the children participated in an over-imitation task and two executive functions tasks (all irrelevant for the current study). The order in which the child completed the perspective-taking task and the task on non-verbal cue understanding was counterbalanced across participants, accounting for gender and language groups. The full procedure was recorded on video. Upon completion of each task, the child received a sticker to add to the sticker-collection card they were given at the start of their visit.

Measures

Visual Perspective-Taking

We measured visual perspective-taking using an adaptation of the director task developed by Fan et al. (2015) and Agostini et al. (2024a). The task consisted of a shelf with 4x4 boxes (10x10 cm), four of which were occluded on the experimenter's side.

Eight objects were placed on the grid, three of which were in privileged boxes (visible only to the child) and five in common ground boxes (visible to both the child and the experimenter) in four different set-ups. These set-ups were counterbalanced across gender and language groups of the participants. In each setup, the child participated in four trials, and the grid was rotated 90° clockwise after each set of trials. One box (16x25 cm) was placed next to the shelf on the child's side. In each trial, the child was asked to remove one item from the shelf and place it in the box. In each setup, the experimenter asked the child to move two unambiguous objects and two ambiguous objects. In unambiguous trials, she asked the child to move objects that were visible to both the child and the experimenter. In the ambiguous trials, the experimenter's instruction could refer to a mutually visible target object or to a distractor object visible only from the child's perspective, see Figure 1. The experimenter wore matte-black sunglasses throughout this task to avoid providing the child with unintended cues through her eye movements. The child's performance on each trial was coded from video by a trained coder.

For unambiguous trials, the coder assigned a score of 1 for selecting the correct object and a 0 for an incorrect object. These trials are not part of the analysis. For the ambiguous trials, the coder coded whether the child selected the target object, the distractor object or another object. Trials in which the child selected neither the target nor the distractor object were coded as invalid trials. Trials in which the child selected the target object were assigned a score of 1; selection of the distractor object was scored as 0. A second trained observer coded the videos from n = 28 children (21% of the sample) using the same procedure. The inter-observer reliability was computed using Cohen's kappa for binary categories (selection of target or distractor). The Kappa value was 0.96, indicating almost perfect (99.8%) agreement between coders (Landis & Koch, 1977). In cases of disagreement between the observers, we used the values reported by the first observer, who coded the entire dataset.

Non-Verbal Cue Understanding

To measure children's non-verbal cue understanding, we adapted the point-or-gaze task, a procedure from Yow and Markman (2011). Two identical opaque boxes (17.5x20.0x9.0 cm) were placed on a table between the experimenter and the child. The boxes were sound-isolated on the inside. The experimenter showed the child a marble, which she then hid in one of the boxes (out of the child's view). She then put the boxes back on the table and indicated the marble's location according to the condition: 1) body-biased; she sat on a chair behind the empty box, 2) body-centred; she sat on a chair between the two boxes, and a) pointing; she pointed with her index finger towards the box containing the toy, gaze directed to a neutral point in the centre of the table, b) gaze: she gazed towards the box containing the marble, her hands resting in her lap. Once the experimenter had taken her position, she asked the child if they could find the marble. If the child chose the correct box, she showed the child the marble and put it in a container next to a fish-shaped music box. If the child chose the wrong box, the experimenter showed the child the empty box, and she kept the marble from the correct box aside. The task consisted of 12 trials (6 body-biased gaze and 2 trials for each of the other three conditions, counterbalanced in four different order series across gender and language groups of participants). After completing the task, the child received all the marbles to put in the music box.

A trained coder coded the child's performance from video, assigning a score of 1 (choosing the box with the marble) or 0 (choosing the empty box). A second trained observer independently coded the videos of n = 28 children (21% of the sample) following the same coding procedure. Inter-observer reliability was assessed using Cohen's kappa for the binary coding categories (selection of target versus distractor).

The resulting kappa coefficient was 0.96, indicating 97.9% agreement and reflecting almost perfect agreement between coders (Landis & Koch, 1977). As in the director task, we used the values from the first coder, who coded the whole dataset, in case of disagreements between coders. As preregistered, we include only the 6 trials in the body-biased position with the gaze-cue, as they elicit understanding of ambiguous (body position) and subtle (gaze) cues (Yow & Markman, 2011).

Language Exposure

In the Language Exposure questionnaire (LEMON -Language Exposure questionnaire for Multilinguals ONline; Openscript GmbH, 2025), caregivers were asked for each caregiving situation since the child's birth, for each day of the week, each interaction partner and each language, and the amount of time the child spends with this interaction partner. Based on all entries, we calculated the proportion of children's awake time, from birth until the day of testing, they have been exposed to each language. Children's language status, as well as the interview on the Social Network Size, was based on caregivers' responses to this questionnaire.

Social Network Size

This parental questionnaire, following Burke et al. (2023), measured the size of the child's social network. We adapted the original questionnaire in two ways. First, rather than asking only about weekly contacts (Burke et al., 2022), we used the child's weekly schedule (i.e., LEMON, see section Language Exposure), as reported by the caregiver, as a starting point for the interview. We then asked caregivers about the demographic information of those individuals (e.g., age, gender, languages) and additional details about the groups (e.g., group size) in which they reported the child participates. Additionally, we asked caregivers to report all other individuals and groups the child interacts with and their demographic information, regardless of frequency, including those not captured in the LEMON (e.g., occasional visitors), who are not part of the child's regular care arrangements. This allowed for the data-driven approach described below (see Exploratory Data Driven Approach). Second, we did not collect information on race or ethnicity of the individuals in the child's social network.

The interview was conducted by phone and was based on caregiver-reported information about the individuals and groups the child interacts with. The interview started based on the information the caregiver reported in the LEMON questionnaire and aimed to extend this information by asking the caregiver to report on all individuals and groups the child interacts with. The SNS questionnaire aimed to provide more detailed information on children's social networks and consisted of 9 questions about each of the individuals/groups the child interacts with regularly, the means of interaction (online or in person), and the characteristics of these people (age and gender), see Table A1 in the Appendix for the full set of questions. The full length of the questionnaire, therefore, depended on the number of individuals/groups that the caregiver indicated their child interacts with. SNS was then defined as the total number of unique "nodes" the child interacts with on a weekly basis (either online or face-to-face), following Burke et al. (2022), as well as through a data-driven approach defining the minimum interaction frequency for individuals/groups to be considered part of the social network (see Exploratory Data Driven Approach). Nodes were defined as individual people the child knows (e.g., parents, nanny) or groups of people (e.g., daycare). Individuals within these groups were only considered individual nodes if they "stood out as friends" or were "caregivers/teachers" based on parental report. This means that children's interactions with children from groups that they did interact with regularly (e.g., in daycare), but were not identified as "friend" by the caregiver, were captured only at the group level, rather than as individual nodes. Further, we calculated the adult ratio in children's weekly network as the number of individuals older than 18 years over the total number of weekly nodes (Burke et al., 2022).

Theory of Mind

Children's Theory of Mind (ToM) was assessed using a digitised version of the Children's Social Understanding Scale (CSUS; Tahiroglu et al., 2014). The CSUS was translated to German in the lab for a previous project and this translation has not been validated. The CSUS comprises 42 questions on a 4-point Likert scale and assesses six ToM subscales: Belief, Knowledge, Perception, Desire, Intention, and Emotion. For the analyses, we use the final score (internal consistency: McDonald's ωtotal = .90), which is calculated as the sum of all item responses divided by the total number of items that received a score.

Analysis

We analysed our data using Generalised Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs). All GLMMs were fitted using the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) in R (R Core Team, 2025). The numerical predictors in all models were standardised to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. The significance level was set at α = .05 (Bakker et al., 2016).

Effects resulting in p-values smaller than .05 were interpreted as statistically significant.

We applied binomial distributions in our models because the outcome variable for both the director task and the point-or-gaze task was binary (the child answered the trial either correctly or incorrectly). We used random intercepts for each child to account for repeated measurements across trials. For the director task, we included fixed effects for social network size (continuous), the setup (4 levels), the trial number (continuous, 1-8), and children's age. For the point-or-gaze task, we included fixed effects for social network size (continuous), trial number (continuous, 1-6), and age. For our exploratory analysis of the association between SNS and ToM, we ran a linear model to predict ToM from SNS, controlling for age.

Following Burke et al. (2023), we conducted an unregistered exploratory analysis relating the number of friends a child has and the adult ratio in their weekly social networks to their performance on the director task (following Burke et al., 2023), and the point-or-gaze task, as well as the CSUS score, by replacing the fixed effect of SNS with the number of friends or adult ratio in the child's weekly social network (continuous).

Exploratory Data Driven Approach.

To explore how associations between SNS and each outcome vary depending on how SNS is operationalised, we conducted an unregistered grid search over interaction frequency thresholds ranging from 1 (at least one contact moment per year) to 365 (daily contact), combined with five-fold grouped cross-validation (Braun et al., 2014). For each threshold, social network size was defined as the number of unique individuals (and groups) with whom a child interacted at or above that frequency. For example, at a threshold of 12 (at least monthly contact), a child who saw their friend weekly (interaction frequency = 52), a cousin twice a month (interaction frequency = 24), and an aunt twice a year (interaction frequency = 2) would have a social network size of 2, since only the friend and the cousin meet the threshold.

We applied this approach to network size only, and not to the other network characteristics adult ratio or number of friends. Model performance was evaluated separately for each outcome: the director task, the point-or-gaze task, and the CSUS questionnaire. For the director task and the point-or-gaze task, we used mean cross-validated log loss as the selection criterion (Murphy, 2012), appropriate for GLMMs with a binomial family. For the CSUS questionnaire, we used the RMSE as the selection criterion, appropriate for linear models assuming Gaussian distributions.

Social network size for each outcome was subsequently recomputed on the full dataset using the corresponding threshold, standardised, and entered into the final GLMMs.

Grid search results across the thresholds within 1 standard deviation from the best and their logloss/RMSE are reported in Table S1 in the supplementary materials and shown in Figure 3.

Results

We excluded four children from all analyses: three because their social network survey was incomplete, and one due to interference from their caregiver during the procedure. We excluded one additional child from the analysis of the director task (final N = 123 because none of their trials of interest was valid. We excluded two additional children from the analysis on the point-of-gaze task due to experimenter error in the procedure (final N = 122).

Before the main analyses, we examined whether counterbalancing order affected performance on the director task and point-or-gaze task, using an ANOVA to predict the proportion score (number of correct trials / total number of valid trials) as a function of counterbalancing order. For the director task, performance did not differ across orders, F (3, 119) = 0.88, p = .453, and order was therefore not included in the analysis. For the point-or-gaze task, however, we observed a significant effect of counterbalancing order on performance, F (3, 125) = 9.78, p < .01, see Table S5 for the post hoc comparisons. Although this check was not preregistered, we included counterbalancing order as a covariate in the model for this task to control for its associations with the outcome variable.

Descriptive Results

On average, children's proportion of correct answers on the director task was 0.35 (SD = 0.30), for the point-or-gaze task 0.64 (SD = 0.27), and the average score on the CSUS was 3.15 (SD = 0.30). Performance on the director task, the point-or-gaze task, and the CSUS did not correlate significantly with one another (all r < .05 and all p > 0.5), see S3 in the supplementary materials.

Social Network Size with Weekly Contact

Children's weekly social network consisted, on average, of 19.4 nodes (SD = 6.99, ranging between 6 and 37 nodes), of which 5.38 were friends (SD = 4.03, ranging between 1 and 21, with n = 7 children for whom the caregiver did not report a friend they have weekly contact with), and the ratio of adults was 0.68 (SD = 0.15, ranging between 0.21 and 1.00).

Visual Perspective-Taking

Children's weekly social network size was not significantly associated with their performance on the director task, B = 0.27, SE = 0.18, OR = 1.31, 95%CI[0.93, 1.86] p = .127, see Figure 2a. Performance on the different setups, however, differed significantly, see Table S6. Full model parameters and confidence intervals are shown in Table A2. Further, neither the adult ratio, B = 0.15, SE = 0.18, OR = 1.16, 95%CI[0.82, 1.65], p = .401 in children's weekly social network size, nor the number of friends, B = 0.33, SE = 0.18, OR = 1.40, 95%CI[0.99, 1.97], p = .058 was significantly associated with their performance on the director task.

Non-Verbal Cue Understanding

Children's weekly social network size was not significantly associated with their performance on the point-or-gaze task (B = -0.05, SE = 0.11, p = 0.635), see Figure 2b. However, children participating in counterbalancing order 3 performed better than children in the other counterbalancing orders, see Table 1 A3.

Theory of Mind

Children's weekly social network size was not significantly associated with their score on the CSUS (B = 0.03, SE = 0.03, p = .266), nor was the adult ratio in their social network or their number of friends measured weekly (p > .468 and p = .084), see Figure 2c and further Table A4 for full model parameters and confidence intervals. (a) Director Task (b) Point-or-Gaze Task (c) CSUS questionnaire Social Network Size with Data-Driven Threshold

We then performed the exploratory grid search, which revealed that SNS-outcome associations were sensitive to how SNS was operationalised, with best-fitting thresholds diverging across outcomes (see supplementary Table S1 and

Figure 3). Therefore, we used each outcome's own best-fitting threshold to operationalise SNS in further analyses.

For visual perspective-taking, measured with the director task, the lowest mean cross-validated log loss was obtained at a threshold of 11 interactions per year, yielding a social network size based on the contacts children have at least approximately once every month. At this threshold, children's social network size consisted of 28.18 nodes (SD = 9.21) and was positively associated with children's visual perspective-taking performance (B = 0.56, SE = 0.18, OR = 1.76, 95%CI[1.25, 2.48], p = .001), meaning that children with larger monthly social networks performed better on the director task, see Figure 4a. Using the same threshold, we found no significant associations between adult ratio and children's number of friends at this interaction frequency (p = .378 and p = .058). The full parameters of these models are reported in Table S4 in the supplementary material.

For non-verbal cue understanding, measured with the point-or-gaze task, the best-fitting threshold was 211 interactions per year, corresponding to approximately 4 For ToM, measured with the CSUS, the best-fitting threshold was markedly higher at 78 interactions per year, reflecting contacts occurring once or twice per week.

With this threshold, children's social network size consisted of, on average, 13.88 nodes (SD = 6.42) and was not significantly correlated to children's score on the CSUS questionnaire (p = .187). See Table A5 for full model parameters for all models.

However, the best-fitting threshold outcome was broader for ToM than for visual perspective-taking and non-verbal cue understanding. A large number of adjacent interaction frequency thresholds produced similar model fit. This indicates that the best-fitting threshold for ToM should be interpreted with caution, as it does not reflect a unique peak but rather a range of similarly fitting models.

Discussion

In the current study, we investigated how diversity in children's social environments is associated with their pragmatic communication behaviour. We assessed 128 preschool children's social network size (using both a conventional and a data-driven approach) and related this to their performance on a visual perspective-taking task, a non-verbal cue understanding task, and their Theory of Mind.

With the conventional approach, we measured the number of individuals and groups the child interacted with on at least a weekly basis (Burke et al., 2022). With this approach, the results showed that SNS was not significantly associated with children's visual perspective-taking, their non-verbal cue understanding, or their Theory of Mind (as reported by their caregiver). Furthermore, characteristics of these social networks, such as the number of friends or the adult ratio, did not correlate with any of the outcome variables. However, SNS was operationalised as a count of individuals and groups, which does not capture the quality or communicative demands of those interactions. Future research should assess interaction quality and content alongside network size.

To further investigate the influence of SNS, we also took a data-driven approach.

This exploratory analysis provided a more differentiated picture: The strength and direction of the association between SNS and each outcome depended on which interaction frequency was used to define SNS. Associations with visual perspective-taking, non-verbal cue understanding, and ToM diverged across thresholds, ranging from positive to negative to non-significant (best-fitting thresholds of 11, 211, and 78 interactions per year, respectively). This does not necessarily imply that each outcome has its own ideal operationalisation of SNS; rather, that different thresholds may capture different aspects of children's social networks (e.g., household composition or frequency of caregiver contact). These different aspects may align differently with each outcome. This approach to operationalising social network size is exploratory, and the reported best-fitting threshold should be treated as a starting point for further research, rather than a confirmatory research outcome. Replication of these results is needed before conclusions can be drawn about how SNS is best operationalised for each outcome.

Visual Perspective-Taking

Contrary to our hypothesis and earlier findings (Burke et al., 2023), we did not find that children's weekly social network size was associated with their visual perspective-taking. Our sensitivity analysis showed that we could only reliably detect effects of OR ≥ 1.50; smaller true associations between weekly SNS and visual perspective-taking may therefore have gone undetected. However, we found that social network size was associated with visual perspective-taking when lowering the minimum interaction frequency threshold from weekly to roughly monthly. This suggests that the operationalisation of social network size is consequential for its effect, and that a broader definition (including less frequent contacts) may better capture the diversity of social experiences that are relevant to perspective-taking development. The contacts the child sees occasionally may provide more diverse social experiences (Granovetter, 1973) and be those who introduce the greatest novelty and diversity in communicative experiences, as the child shares the least common ground with them (Bohn & Köymen, 2018; Wermelinger et al., 2024). In contrast, frequent contacts are likely to share a large amount of common ground with the child, reducing the need to infer the communicative partner's perspective. Including the more infrequent contacts could therefore provide a more representative picture of the social diversity a child encounters in their daily life (Burke et al., 2022).

Neither the adult ratio in the social network nor the number of friends was associated with children's visual perspective-taking, and this pattern was consistent when using the data-driven operationalisation of social network size (11 interactions per year threshold). For preschool children, adults may pose more challenging interaction partners than peers: adults use less simplified speech and assume more perspective-taking (Mauritzson & Säljö, 2001), whereas conversations with peers are more symmetrical and collaborative (Blum-Kulka & Snow, 2004). Our findings, therefore, are in contrast with arguments that adult interlocutors may provide perspective-taking practice, which would lead to enhanced perspective-taking skills (Lewis et al., 1996). One possible explanation is that the quality or diversity of interactions, rather than the characteristics of the individual, is more important for perspective-taking. Alternatively, the adult ratio as measured here may not capture the nature of adult-child interactions. A higher proportion of adults in a child's network does not necessarily imply more communicatively challenging exchanges; interactions with familiar adults, such as parents or regular caregivers, may be no more cognitively challenging from a perspective-taking standpoint than interactions with familiar peers or older children (Tomasello, 2003).

Children's number of correct responses in the director task measuring visual perspective-taking was notably low, but consistent with prior work showing that visual perspective-taking remains challenging for children, even in Level I tasks (Brezack et al., 2021; Burke et al., 2023). For example, 3-year-olds account for their communicative partner's perspective when asked for an object visible to both of them, but perform inconsistently when asked for an object outside of the partner's view (Brezack et al., 2021). Adults, even when informed of what is visible to the director and what is not, make egocentric errors in a director task (Keysar et al., 2000). The low performance in our sample, therefore, likely reflects the difficulty of visual perspective-taking, rather than a floor effect. This is further supported by varying performance across different task setups; some setups were more challenging than others, indicating that performance was sensitive to task demands rather than uniform.

Specifically, the order in which the ambiguous and unambiguous trials were presented in the two setups on which children performed best (setup D and B) was compartmentalised (set up D: Ambiguous -Unambiguous -Unambiguous -Ambiguous and set up B: Unambiguous -Unambiguous -Ambiguous -Ambiguous) vs interleaved in the two set ups children performed worse on (set up A and C: Unambiguous -Ambiguous -Unambiguous -Ambiguous). Nonetheless, low and variable performance, as well as task-related noise, may have masked meaningful associations between SNS and perspective-taking, and it may have affected our power to detect these associations.

Non-Verbal Cue Understanding

Contrary to our hypothesis, neither the weekly social network size, the adult ratio, nor the number of friends was associated with children's performance on the point-or-gaze task. The same power constraint applies here: our design could only reliably detect effects of OR ≥ 1.36, so a true but smaller association with weekly SNS cannot be ruled out. The same power constraint applies here: our design could only reliably detect effects of OR ≥ 1.50, so a true but smaller association with weekly SNS cannot be ruled out. Our data-driven approach, however, revealed a notable pattern: when SNS was operationalised using a threshold of approximately 4 interactions per week, it was negatively associated with non-verbal cue understanding. That is, children who interacted very frequently with a larger number of people performed worse on the task.

This finding stands in contrast to the hypothesis we derived from the COME perspective (Wermelinger et al., 2024) and to evidence of communicative advantages in bilingual children (Lauro et al., 2020; Yow & Markman, 2011), which indicate that bilingualism is positively associated with understanding non-verbal cues. Here, we hypothesised that diversity in the communicative environment, rather than language status per se, would drive the differences in the communicative behaviour of monolingual and bilingual children. The results, however, show that greater diversity in social experiences, as approximated by a larger social network, was associated with poorer performance.

One explanation is that highly familiar communication partners develop partner-specific knowledge of how communicative cues, such as pointing or gazing, are used (Rohlfing et al., 2017). This is similar to the concept of idiolect and family dialect: the unique communicative behaviour and language use that emerge within relationships or families (Van Mensel, 2018). Just as families develop shared communicative patterns, with specific words and references that are hard for outsiders to interpret, children may become attuned to their caregivers' gestures. This is supported by the results that infants are more responsive and learn more effectively from a familiar partner's gaze and referential cues than from those of strangers (Begus et al., 2016; Hoehl et al., 2012).

Children in smaller, possibly denser networks may therefore be exposed to the same cues and communication patterns over and over again, training their awareness of and attention to non-verbal cues more than children who experience greater variability in the cues they observe, which they can then apply in lab-based tasks.

An alternative interpretation is that the best-fitting threshold for this task (i.e., 4 times a week) defines a network that reflects the most frequent contacts in the child's life: immediate family members (parents and siblings), other caregivers (daycare teachers), and other close contacts (e.g., best friend). Network size, operationalised in this way, may no longer capture social diversity at all, but instead reflect family structure, such as number of siblings. An unregistered exploratory check supported this: network size at this threshold correlated positively with children's number of siblings (r = .24, p = .009), but was unrelated to whether children attended daycare in generalfoot_0 (t(118) = 0.76, p = .449).

This suggests that household composition, rather than external caregiving arrangements. Caregivers with more children need to distribute their attention across each one of them. This may limit the development of partner-specific communication patterns with each child. In contrast, children with fewer siblings spend more time with each caregiver and train their sensitivity to their partner-specific cues more strongly, which they may be able to transfer to a novel partner in a lab setting. Family size is associated with children's social-cognitive development more broadly (Devine & Hughes, 2018). The negative association between network size and non-verbal cue understanding may, therefore, reflect associations between household composition and non-verbal cue understanding rather than social diversity. The two interpretations could occur simultaneously; both suggest, through different pathways, that larger high-frequency network size reduces children's opportunities to develop sensitivity to partner-specific non-verbal communicative cues (Begus et al., 2016; Hoehl et al., 2012). Future research that simultaneously examines household composition, caregiving arrangements (e.g., co-parenting, three-generation households), and network density could disentangle these options.

Finally, the significant effect of counterbalancing order warrants careful interpretation of the results. Children randomly assigned to order 3 performed considerably better than children in other counterbalancing orders. To explain this difference, we compared the counterbalancing groups on several variables (gender, age, experimenter, and month of testing) and found no significant differences among the four groups (see Figure S1 in the supplements). One possible, yet weak explanation for this effect is that children in this counterbalancing order were the only group to see a body-biased trial (with pointing) as their first trial, directly followed by a body-biased gaze trial (of interest). Possibly, children learned in this first trial that they need to ignore the experimenter's body position and interpret the other cue only to find the marble. However, this would suggest that children in the other groups would have improved performance on their trials of interest after their first body-biased point trial, an effect we did not find.

In short, the results for non-verbal cue understanding do not support the hypothesis that larger social networks enhance children's understanding of ambiguous non-verbal cues. The data-driven results suggest the opposite pattern for high-frequency contacts. We interpret this as either a result of specialisation arising from high-frequency interactions or as an artefact of the operationalisation of social network size. Future research could directly examine the roles of partner familiarity and the composition of children's high-frequency networks in non-verbal cue understanding.

Theory of Mind

Neither weekly social nor data-driven network (based on roughly 1-2 interactions per week) size or characteristics (adult ratio, number of friends) were associated with children's ToM as reported by their caregivers on the CSUS (Tahiroglu et al., 2014).

This is in contrast with the general assumption that more varied social environments support the development of ToM (Hughes & Leekam, 2004; Lewis et al., 1996). Our sensitivity analysis suggests we could only reliably detect effects of Cohen's f2 ≥ 0.06, so a smaller association between SNS and ToM remain possible.

However, other work suggests that the relationship between social experiences and ToM is more nuanced than SNS can capture (Devine & Hughes, 2018). Caregiver sensitivity, shared pretend play, and talk about mental states within close relationships are stronger predictors of ToM than SNS (Adrián et al., 2005; Cutting & Dunn, 1999; Ensor & Hughes, 2008), suggesting that ToM is more sensitive to the quality of social relationships than to their quantity. These qualitatively distinct experiences within close relationships are not captured by SNS (Dunn et al., 1991; Slaughter et al., 2007).

The divergence between results for ToM and visual perspective-taking requires specific attention, as visual perspective-taking is a component of the broader ToM construct (Flavell, 2004; Wellman, 2014). The two measures tap different levels of the ToM hierarchy and differ in methodology, and both distinctions are relevant here. The director task targets a specific perceptual process: inferring what is currently visible to another person, and is performance-based in a single time-controlled lab setting. The CSUS asks caregivers to report on higher-order competencies, including reasoning about beliefs, intentions, and emotions in everyday contexts, summarised across the preceding weeks (Wellman & Liu, 2004). These higher-order competencies may depend less on network size and more on the quality of specific interactions, particularly talk about mental states (Ensor & Hughes, 2008; Ruffman et al., 2002). Furthermore, performance-based and caregiver-report measures of social cognition exhibit only modest convergent validity in early childhood (Dore et al., 2015), and in the present sample, none of the three tasks correlated with one another (see Results). This supports the view that they assess partially distinct constructs, amplified here by the difference between a single lab-based task and a retrospective caregiver report. The null result in ToM may therefore reflect insensitivity of the measure to variation in social exposure, rather than an absence of associations between social experiences and ToM.

Limitations and Methodological Considerations

Several limitations should be considered. First, in the operationalisation of the social network measure, individuals within groups were counted as nodes. Following Relatedly, social network size relied on parent report; parents may struggle to accurately recall interaction frequency, and no validation studies currently support this method for young children. Future work could aim to better capture the number and variety of peer interactions within group settings, rather than relying on caregiver judgment (Legendre & Munchenbach, 2011).

Second, the exploratory data-driven approach searched interaction thresholds across the full range of 1 to 365 (once a year to daily), without constraints on the resulting network composition. This threshold may have captured overly narrow networks. We used 5-fold cross-validation to reduce overfitting, but this does not fully eliminate the possibility that thresholds reflect sample-specific characteristics. Future work could instead constrain the threshold search to a theoretically motivated range, for example excluding thresholds that would capture only the immediate household. This would ensure that any threshold identified as best fitting would still capture diversity arising from larger social networks, rather than caregiving arrangements.

Third, the cross-sectional design limits causal claims and the predominantly high SES sample may limit generalisability, given that SES may relate to caregiving arrangements and network composition (Bussing et al., 2003; G. Bouchard et al., 2025), as well as to ToM (Morales & Farkas, 2025).

Finally, the present study focused on social network size as a source of communicative diversity independent of language background. Therefore, we did not assess or control for children's language status. Given that language status could relate to performance on the pragmatic communication tasks (e.g., Fan et al., 2015; Yow & Markman, 2011) studied here, future work should examine whether the present associations hold when accounting for language background.

Conclusion

The present findings extend previous work in two directions: measuring social network size in preschoolers as a source of diversity in children's everyday environment and relating this to their communicative and pragmatic outcomes.

Taken together, the results suggest that how social network size is operationalised matters: associations with children's communicative and pragmatic outcomes varied, and in some cases reversed direction, depending on the interaction frequency used to define the social network. This suggests that different operationalisations may capture different underlying constructs (e.g., social diversity, caregiving arrangements, household composition), each differently associated with children's development. Future research should systematically investigate which features of children's social networks (e.g., frequency, diversity, relationship quality) best distinguish these constructs and most robustly predict developmental and behavioural outcomes across samples and tasks.

We demonstrated that the association between social network size and visual perspective-taking and non-verbal cue understanding is sensitive to how the network is operationalised.

For full model parameters and confidence intervals, see Table

Figure 2

Figure 2Model-estimated probability of correct responses (director-and point-or-gaze task) and final score (CSUS) as a function of social network size (z-scored). Shaded area represents 95% confidence intervals.

Figure 3

Figure 3 Logloss/RMSE for social network size calculated for each interaction frequency. Lower values indicate better predictive fit. The dashed vertical line indicates the best-fitting threshold (11 for the director task, 211 for the point-or-gaze task, and 78 for CSUS).

(a) Director Task (b) Point-or-Gaze Task (c) CSUS questionnaire interactions per week. At this threshold, children's social network had a mean size of 4.16 nodes (SD = 3.30), and may reflect children's household composition, rather than social network diversity (see Discussion). Social network size, calculated at this threshold, correlated negatively with children's performance on the point-or-gaze task (B = -0.21, SE = 0.10, OR = 0.81, 95%CI[0.66, 0.99], p = .039), see Figure 4b. This means that children with larger social network sizes had lower scores on the point-or-gaze task, when SNS was defined as the number of nodes the child interacted with around 4 times a week.

Director Task(b) Point-or-Gaze Task (c) CSUS questionnaire

Burke et al. (2022), children's interactions with daycare peers were only counted as individual nodes when they "stood out as friends" to the caregiver, or when the individual was a caregiver or teacher. Otherwise, these interactions were captured only at the group level. This decision may undercount the diversity of a child's interactions within groups, since children in group care settings likely engage with peers who do not stand out as friends to a caregiver, but nonetheless contribute to the communicative demands placed on the child (National Research Council (US) & Institute of Medicine (US) Committee on Integrating the Science of Early ChildhoodDevelopment, 2000).
